questions.question: In a barter economy where goods are directly exchanged without the use of money, which essential condition must be satisfied?
options: Double coincidence of wants (both parties must agree to sell and buy each other's commodities)
A formal promissory guarantee certified by the village panchayat
Gold coins deposited with an escrow magistrate
A fixed exchange price list published by the state government
questions.explanation: In an ancient barter economy where commodities are exchanged directly without any monetary medium, exchange is constrained by the 'double coincidence of wants'. This means that what one party desires to sell must coincide precisely with what the other party wishes to buy (e.g. a shoemaker needing wheat must find a wheat farmer wanting shoes). Because searching for matching reciprocal trading partners is exceedingly difficult, time-consuming, and inefficient, the introduction of money revolutionized commerce by eliminating this obstacle.

questions.question: Why is money referred to as a 'medium of exchange'?
options: Because it is minted exclusively from precious silver and gold bullion
Because it acts as an intermediary instrument in the transactions and exchange of goods and services
Because it can only be exchanged inside foreign diplomatic embassies
Because it changes its face value automatically every month
questions.explanation: Money is termed a 'medium of exchange' because it acts as a universally accepted intermediary asset in the purchase and sale of goods, assets, and services. In a modern economy, a person holding money does not have to search for double coincidences; they can immediately purchase any commodity or service desired from any merchant. By decoupling the act of sale from the act of purchase, money solves the indivisibility and storage problems of barter, serving as a universal standard unit of account and store of economic value.

questions.question: Unlike historical money (such as grain, cattle, gold, and silver coins), modern Indian currency:
options: Can be eaten as nutritious food during famines
Is valid only within 5 kilometers of the Reserve Bank headquarters
Must be redeemed for silver bullion at the post office every year
Is not made of precious metal and has virtually no intrinsic everyday value of its own
questions.explanation: Historically, early forms of money possessed intrinsic commodity value—such as cattle, grain, or coins minted from precious bullion like gold, silver, and copper. In contrast, modern currency (paper banknotes and metal token coins) has virtually zero intrinsic physical value: a ₹500 paper banknote has negligible raw material worth. Modern currency functions successfully as money purely because it is 'fiat money'—it is legally authorized, guaranteed, and decreed as legal tender by the sovereign authority of the central government.

questions.question: In India, which central authority is legally authorized by law to issue currency notes on behalf of the Central Government?
options: The State Bank of India (SBI)
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
The Ministry of Heavy Industries
questions.explanation: In the Republic of India, under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the sole central monetary authority legally empowered to issue currency notes on behalf of the Central Government. As per Indian law, no other commercial bank, private corporation, state government, or private individual is permitted to issue currency. Every RBI banknote bears the signature of the RBI Governor and a sovereign promise: 'I promise to pay the bearer the sum of... Guarantee of the Central Government' (NCERT Section 3.1).

questions.question: Why cannot any individual or merchant legally refuse a payment made in Indian Rupees for settling a transaction in India?
options: Because bank notes contain microchips tracked by police satellites
Because the law legalizes the use of Rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions in India
Because merchants are paid a commission by the World Bank on every note
Because all shopkeepers are government civil service employees
questions.explanation: The Indian Rupee (INR) is legally declared as universal 'legal tender' by parliamentary statute. Indian law establishes that currency notes and coins issued by the Reserve Bank of India constitute a valid medium of payment that cannot be lawfully refused by any citizen, business, or merchant in the settlement of debts and commercial transactions within Indian territory. Refusing to accept legal tender in settlement of a lawful monetary debt is an illegal act under the Coinage Act and the Reserve Bank of India Act.

questions.question: Why are deposits in bank savings or current accounts referred to as 'Demand Deposits'?
options: Because the government demands 90% of the deposit as income tax
Because the depositor must file an application in court before withdrawing money
Because the deposited money can be withdrawn by the depositor on demand at any time
Because banks demand that depositors keep gold bullion in their lockers
questions.explanation: Individuals and commercial businesses deposit surplus cash into bank accounts for safety and to earn interest. Because the funds held in savings and current bank accounts can be withdrawn or transferred by the account holder 'on demand' at any time—via bank branch cash counters, ATMs, cheques, or electronic fund transfers (NEFT/RTGS/UPI)—these deposits are technically classified as 'Demand Deposits'. Demand deposits share the essential characteristics of cash, functioning as a primary component of the modern money supply.

questions.question: A cheque is best defined as:
options: A government tax receipt confirming property ownership
A currency note printed by commercial private banks
A postal telegram ordering delivery of agricultural goods
A paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the drawer's account to the person in whose name the cheque has been issued
questions.explanation: A cheque is a negotiable banking instrument in paper form instructing a bank to pay a specific sum of money from the account of the person writing the cheque (the drawer) to the person, business, or entity in whose name the instrument has been drawn (the payee). Cheques allow large financial transactions, business trade settlements, and debt clearances to occur seamlessly between bank accounts without the physical handling, transport, or risk of carrying bulky paper banknotes (NCERT Class 10 Economics Chapter 3).

questions.subtopic: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) of Commercial Banks
questions.question: Roughly what proportion of their total deposits do commercial banks in India keep as liquid cash to meet daily withdrawal demands of depositors?
options: About 15% of their total deposits
100% of their total deposits
Less than 0.1% of their deposits
Exactly 75% of their deposits
questions.explanation: Under statutory guidelines enforced by the Reserve Bank of India (Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio), commercial banks keep only a small fraction of their total deposits—typically about 15 percent—as liquid cash reserves. Historical banking data shows that on any given business day, only a small fraction of depositors come to withdraw money. Holding ~15% liquid cash is mathematically sufficient to honor daily withdrawals, allowing banks to utilize the remaining 85% of deposits to extend loans to borrowers.

questions.subtopic: Main Source of Income for Commercial Banks
questions.question: What constitutes the primary source of income for commercial banks?
options: Monetary grants received every month from the United Nations
Profits earned from selling real estate properties
The difference between the higher interest rate charged on loans to borrowers and the lower interest rate paid to depositors
Municipal fees collected from printing currency notes
questions.explanation: Commercial banks act as financial intermediaries between depositors who have surplus funds and borrowers who require credit for investment. Banks pay a modest interest rate to depositors on their savings and fixed deposits (e.g. 4%–6% per annum). Simultaneously, banks lend these deposited funds to borrowers at a significantly higher interest rate (e.g. 9%–14% per annum). The financial spread—the difference between the interest charged on loans and the interest paid to depositors—constitutes the primary operating income of banks.

questions.question: In the NCERT case of Salim, a shoe manufacturer receiving a festival order for 3,000 pairs of shoes, how did credit impact his business?
options: It enabled him to procure raw materials, hire extra workers, fulfill the contract on time, earn good profits, and repay the loan
It forced him to sell his family ancestral home and become a landless labourer
It resulted in criminal prosecution and bankruptcy
It caused him to abandon leather shoe manufacturing completely
questions.explanation: A debt-trap occurs when a borrower takes credit that does not generate sufficient income to cover repayment, forcing them into a worsening cycle of indebtedness. For instance, in agriculture (as in the NCERT case of Swapna), if a crop fails due to pests or drought, the farmer cannot repay the seasonal loan. To survive and service the debt, the farmer is forced to borrow more at exorbitant informal rates or sell off productive land assets. Rather than improving their financial position, credit pushes the borrower into distress.

questions.explanation: Collateral is a tangible physical or financial asset owned by the borrower—such as agricultural land, a house, commercial property, vehicle, gold jewellery, or fixed deposits with banks—that the borrower pledges to the lender as a security guarantee for a loan. If the borrower defaults and fails to repay the credit, the lender has the legal right to repossess and liquidate the pledged collateral to recover the unpaid principal and accrued interest. Pledging collateral mitigates the lender's credit default risk.

questions.question: 'Collateral' in a loan agreement is defined as:
options: A cash bribe paid to the bank manager to approve the loan application
An asset that the borrower owns (such as land, building, vehicle, livestock, bank deposits) and pledges to the lender as a guarantee until the loan is repaid
A certificate of good conduct issued by the local member of parliament
An insurance policy against foreign currency fluctuations
questions.explanation: Every formal or informal loan agreement is governed by the 'terms of credit', which specify four mandatory components: (1) The specific interest rate charged on the principal amount; (2) Collateral security required to guarantee the loan; (3) Documentation requirements verifying the borrower's identity, income, and employment; (4) The mode of repayment (e.g. monthly EMIs, bullet lump-sum, cash or bank transfer). The terms of credit vary widely depending on the nature of the lender and the creditworthiness of the borrower.

questions.question: Which four components together constitute the 'Terms of Credit' in any formal lending transaction?
options: Political party membership, caste certificate, passport, and driving license
Interest rate, collateral, documentation required, and mode of repayment
Gold jewellery, silver coins, foreign currency, and postal stamps
Tax audit reports, company balance sheet, factory blueprint, and electricity bill
questions.explanation: In India, credit is bifurcated into two sectors: (1) Formal sector: Commercial banks and cooperatives regulated by the RBI, which charge fair, regulated interest rates (usually 8% to 12% per year) but require collateral and strict documentation; (2) Informal sector: Village moneylenders, traders, and relatives who demand no asset collateral or paperwork, but charge usurious interest rates (often 36% to 60%+ annually) and frequently deploy exploitative or coercive recovery practices, trapping poor rural families in chronic poverty.

options: Village moneylenders and agricultural traders
Friends, neighbours, and relatives
Employers and local commission agents
Commercial Banks and Cooperative Societies
questions.explanation: The formal credit sector in India comprises institutional lending entities that are registered with and supervised by the government, primarily commercial banks (public sector banks like SBI, private banks) and rural cooperative credit societies. questions.question: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans. Which of the following is a key objective of this supervision?
options: Ordering banks to charge a 50% interest rate on rural agricultural loans
Forbidding banks from keeping any liquid cash reserves in their vaults
Ensuring that banks give loans not only to profit-making businesses and rich traders, but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries, and small borrowers
Prohibiting commercial banks from opening branches in rural areas
questions.explanation: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) exercises statutory supervision over the formal banking sector to achieve multiple policy objectives: (1) Ensuring that banks actually maintain minimum cash reserve ratios; (2) Monitoring loan allocations through mandatory Priority Sector Lending (PSL) targets, ensuring commercial credit flows to small farmers, rural artisans, and small-scale entrepreneurs rather than flowing exclusively to wealthy corporate conglomerates; (3) Regulating transparent interest rates and capital adequacy norms.

questions.question: Why is borrowing from the informal credit sector (moneylenders) frequently disastrous for poor rural households?
options: There is no supervisory organization, interest rates are exorbitantly high (often 3% to 5% per month), and lenders use coercive recovery methods
Moneylenders require three government identity cards and a university diploma
Informal loans must be repaid in British Pounds Sterling
Moneylenders are legally barred from lending cash to farmers
questions.explanation: Borrowing from informal moneylenders is frequently devastating for vulnerable households because: (1) There is no regulatory agency overseeing informal credit activities or capping usurious interest rates (which can reach 60% per year); (2) High borrowing costs consume most of the debtor's agricultural income, leaving little for subsistence; (3) Informal lenders frequently deploy manipulative record-keeping, harassment, and coercive seizure of land and livestock to enforce repayment, cementing generational bonded indebtedness.

questions.question: A typical Self-Help Group (SHG) organized in rural India consists of how many members, meeting and pooling their savings regularly?
options: 15 to 20 members, usually belonging to one neighbourhood
500 to 1,000 members from different districts
Only 2 members (a husband and wife)
Exactly 100 registered company directors
questions.explanation: A standard Self-Help Group (SHG) organized in rural India consists of 15 to 20 members, usually women belonging to one local village neighbourhood, who meet and pool their savings on a regular weekly or monthly basis. Individual savings typically range from ₹25 to ₹100 or more per meeting, depending on members' economic capacity. Members can take small, low-interest loans from the group's pooled corpus to meet immediate family needs (such as medical treatment, seeds, or school fees) without falling prey to village moneylenders.

questions.question: How do Self-Help Groups solve the problem of 'lack of collateral' for rural poor women seeking bank loans?
options: The members mortgage their ancestral village farmland to foreign investors
The panchayat sarpanch signs a blank cheque on behalf of the group
After regular savings for a year or two, the group becomes eligible for bank loans sanctioned in the name of the group without requiring individual asset collateral
The Reserve Bank directly deposits ₹10 lakh into each member's personal account
questions.explanation: The greatest structural hurdle preventing rural poor women from securing formal bank loans is the complete absence of physical asset collateral. Self-Help Groups (SHGs) resolve this impasse through collective social guarantee: when an SHG maintains disciplined savings and financial records for one to two years, commercial banks sanction microcredit directly in the collective name of the group without requiring individual collateral. All members are jointly responsible for timely repayment, guaranteeing high recovery rates.

questions.question: The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh, which successfully pioneered micro-credit for millions of poor women, was founded by Nobel Peace laureate:
options: Amartya Sen
Professor Muhammad Yunus
Manmohan Singh
Abhijit Banerjee
questions.explanation: The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh was founded in the 1970s by economist Professor Muhammad Yunus, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006 for pioneering micro-credit and micro-finance. Starting as a modest research project, Grameen Bank demonstrated that even the poorest rural women, possessing zero physical collateral, are highly creditworthy and reliable entrepreneurs when organized into micro-credit circles. By 2018, Grameen Bank served over 9 million low-income borrowers across 81,600 villages throughout Bangladesh.
